resolutions: An absolutive NNC contains a nounstem predicate and no tense position.
English tense, copular wording, and definite or indefinite articles come from translation context; the application does not invent them.
The nounstem may identify, describe, or locate, but referentiality belongs to the subject personal pronoun.
Cultural nounstem animacy normally guides interpretation, but actual subject reference is the deciding grammatical factor.
Animate reference allows singular or plural subject number; nonanimate reference uses common number unless metaphorical use is chosen.
Common number does not encode an English count versus mass distinction and may be translated singular or plural according to context.
The Number position belongs to the NNC subject and is never nounstem inflection.
A singular-meaning nounstem may predicate a plural subject because subject and predicate remain separate constituents.
Most nounstems permit either State; only typed lexical authority may restrict State, and the visible cue for that restriction is exception.
Lesson 12 reuses State, Subject, Animacy, Metaphorical use, and Full paradigm; it adds no connector, tense, article, or noun-plural control.
